answer.exemplar: The two accounts make opposite predictions about the same neighbourhood. The deficit account treats the settlement as an output of state failure: the city did not plan for the arrivals, did not supply land or services, and the households filled the gap, so the settlement should shrink once the state provides adequately, and officials who describe it as self-sufficient are evading their duty. The exclusion account treats the settlement as a constrained choice: formal land is priced beyond what a low-wage household can pay, mortgages and rental contracts are unavailable without documents, and so the only live option is to build where people already are, which means the settlement should persist until the terms of the formal market change rather than until the will to provide changes. Each misleads at its own edge. The deficit account becomes an excuse when it stops asking why the formal market excluded the households it praises for coping, because provision at prices the residents cannot meet is not provision. The exclusion account becomes an excuse when it treats the absence of alternatives as a free preference, because a choice among what remains available is not the same as a choice, and it can also romanticise arrangements with high mortality and no secure tenure. The productive use of both is to ask which prices and which rules produced the settlement, since that is what a policy would have to change.

questions.explanation: This item tests the value of holding two explanations of the same settlement apart, because they imply different policies and different judgments about the residents. The deficit account predicts that households take what is offered and that provision would shrink the settlement; the exclusion account predicts that households build where land and lending are reachable and that formal provision would be unreachable at their incomes. Each misleads when treated as the whole story: the deficit account when it excuses the state and ignores the price of formal land, the exclusion account when it treats a constrained choice as free preference.
questions.hint: Ask what each account expects to see, and what it cannot see.
questions.learningObjective: compare deficit and choice accounts of informal settlement

answer.exemplar: A reform can be entirely correct at the revenue stage and still leave the resident's experience untouched, so the useful analysis is to follow the chain from the new tax to the service and ask where it breaks. Four breaks are common. The yield may be smaller than the estimates, because a digitised register records what is already known rather than what has been built, and the unregistered part of the city is precisely the part that has the least cash; a new rate on a narrow base raises little. The money may be absorbed, because a city with deferred maintenance and a payroll it cannot meet will use the new revenue to pay arrears and salaries before it repairs a clinic, and it will say it is honouring the reform. The money may be spent elsewhere, because earmarking a revenue does not earmark a decision, and a capital project that opens a road competes with the service the reform was meant to improve. And the binding constraint may not be revenue at all: a water connection needs a maintenance budget, a trained worker and a functioning supply, and where those are missing, more money changes the price of inputs rather than the number of people served. So the honest test of a finance reform is not whether the revenue arrived but whether the specific service a resident uses got better, and if it did not, the failure is somewhere in that chain rather than in the tax.

questions.explanation: This item tests the distinction between a reform of municipal finance and a reform of service delivery, since money reaching a city is not the same as a resident meeting a service. The reform can fail because the new yield is absorbed by existing costs, because the register and the rate are wrong, because the money is spent on capital rather than on the service in question, or because the binding constraint is staff and maintenance rather than revenue. A complete answer identifies where the chain breaks rather than assuming the extra money was the missing part.
questions.hint: Ask what stands between a new revenue stream and a better service.
questions.learningObjective: explain the reasons a fiscal reform does not improve service quality
